candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the `redirect_uri` request parameter submitted to `/change_email.do` (and rendered into the `/change_email` page), the `client_id` parameter, and the `/verify_email?code=...` link that is delivered to the victim (the code is e-mailed to an address the attacker chose during `beginEmailChange`). The attacker needs an account of their own (any authenticated user may start an email change) and a client_id whose client details have no `change_email_redirect_url` additional information — which is the default for clients not bootstrapped with that property.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Registered redirect patterns are still honoured first, so when the requested URI matches a client registration (or the client defines `change_email_redirect_url`) the returned value is legitimate; the account-creation/reset-password/invitation flows pass non-null fallbacks and are not affected; `ChangeEmailEndpoints` (JSON API) never uses the request-supplied URI; the login success handler validates `form_redirect_uri` against the request host (`UaaUrlUtils.uriHasMatchingHost`, `UaaSavedRequestCache.shouldSaveFormRedirectParameter`), which blocks the *anonymous* branch from redirecting off-host — only the authenticated branch (raw `redirect:` view) is unmediated. Existing tests `ChangeEmailControllerTest#testVerifyEmailWithRedirectUrl` and `#testVerifyEmailWithRedirectWhenAuthenticated` (lines 224-272) currently assert the weak behaviour (`redirectedUrl("//example.com/callback")`), i.e. they encode rather than contradict the flaw, so they cannot be used to show the behaviour is forbidden.
candidates.impact: Open redirect issued from the trusted UAA origin: an attacker can craft a UAA-hosted link that forwards an authenticated user to an arbitrary external site, enabling credible phishing and link laundering (e.g., a link that looks like a legitimate UAA e-mail-verification link and lands on an attacker page). It also leaks a trusted Referer/URL context to the attacker. No credential/token theft was demonstrated from this path alone; impact is constrained to redirection-based abuse.
candidates.prerequisites: 1) Attacker is authenticated (own account) and calls POST /change_email.do with `client_id=<client without change_email_redirect_url>` and `redirect_uri=<attacker URL>`; 2) the resulting expiring code is captured from the e-mail sent to the attacker-chosen new address (not clicked by the attacker); 3) the victim is logged in to the UAA and opens the crafted `https://<uaa>/verify_email?code=<code>` link; 4) the code is still valid (30-minute lifetime per EMAIL_CHANGE_LIFETIME).
candidates.root_cause: `UaaUrlUtils.findMatchingRedirectUri` returns the *requested* redirect URI verbatim when no registered pattern matches AND the supplied fallback is null (`return ofNullable(fallbackRedirectUri).orElse(requestedRedirectUri)` — the Javadoc at UaaUrlUtils.java:96 explicitly names this the 'OPEN REDIRECT' case). `EmailChangeEmailService.completeVerification` passes a fallback that is normally absent — `clientDetails.getAdditionalInformation().get(CHANGE_EMAIL_REDIRECT_URL)` ('change_email_redirect_url'), which ordinary clients do not define — and the requested value was previously taken from the caller's `redirect_uri` request parameter and stored in the expiring code (`EmailChangeEmailService.beginEmailChange`, lines 78/87-94). The controller then uses the resulting string as a raw redirect target: `ChangeEmailController.verifyEmail` returns `"redirect:" + redirectLocation` for authenticated callers (and appends it to the public `/login?...&form_redirect_uri=` URL for anonymous callers). Sibling flows in the same codebase avoid this by passing a non-null default (UaaResetPasswordService.java:130-141 uses "home"; EmailAccountCreationService.java:129 uses signup_redirect_url or "home"; EmailInvitationsService.java:72-76 uses "/home") or by never trusting the request-supplied URI (ChangeEmailEndpoints.java:90-105 only uses the configured value).
candidates.title: Open redirect in email-change verification (/verify_email) because the redirect allowlist is bypassed when the client's change_email_redirect_url is absent
candidates.trace: POST /change_email.do (client_id, redirect_uri) -> EmailChangeController.changeEmail -> EmailChangeEmailService.beginEmailChange -> generateExpiringCode stores the raw `redirect_uri` in the expiring-code data (lines 87-94) -> attacker obtains the code from the e-mail to the new address and sends the /verify_email link to the victim -> ChangeEmailController.verifyEmail -> EmailChangeEmailService.completeVerification (lines 115-129): client has no `change_email_redirect_url`, so `findMatchingRedirectUri(registeredRedirectUris, "<attacker URL>", null)` returns the attacker URL because the fallback is null -> `response.put("redirect_url", redirectLocation)` -> for a session carrying UaaAuthentication the controller returns `"redirect:" + redirectLocation` (line 126), producing an HTTP 302 whose Location is the attacker-controlled absolute URL; for anonymous sessions the same value is placed in the trusted `/login?...&form_redirect_uri=` URL (line 131).
candidates.unverified: No execution, build, or test run was performed (source review only), so the chain was not runtime-confirmed. I could not determine whether every deployment's clients lack `change_email_redirect_url` (the exploit needs at least one such client and a victim session), nor whether the VUL4J-40 ground-truth defect is this specific path. The exact browser handling of the produced Location value (absolute vs protocol-relative) was reasoned from Spring's RedirectView behaviour, not observed.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-601 Open Redirect (improper validation of a redirect target before use)

coverage_summary: Reviewed the assigned 1746-file source snapshot (modules: `model`, `server`, `uaa` web resources/XML, `metrics-data`, `samples`), reading in depth the OAuth/authorization endpoint, redirect resolvers, account creation/email-change/reset-password/invitation flows, SCIM user/group endpoints, token services and revocation/listing endpoints, filters (CORS, zone switching/resolving, saved-request, MFA, CSRF), and the Spring Security XML chains (`oauth-endpoints.xml`, `scim-endpoints.xml`, `client-admin-endpoints.xml`, `multitenant-endpoints.xml`, `login-ui.xml`, `spring-servlet.xml`). The P1 relation index covers 747 of 1276 Java files with no data-flow/control-flow or semantic resolution (87,672 unresolved calls), so every candidate was confirmed against source text; index labels were used only for navigation. Tests were read as behavioural documentation, not run. The `docs/` folder, build files (`build.gradle`, `shared_versions.gradle`) and third-party library internals were not audited line by line.
limitations: No code was executed, built, or tested; no runtime/exploit confirmation exists for any candidate.
The P1 index is partial (747/1276 Java files parsed, no data flow, no runtime reachability, 87,672 unresolved calls); unreported areas were not treated as reviewed.

Third-party library behaviour that the finding depends on (Spring's `RedirectView` handling of absolute URLs, `DefaultRedirectResolver` sub-domain matching) was not inspected in library source; where it matters, I relied on the repository's own tests and on Spring semantics only.

The full reasoning about the exploit chain requires an attacker-controlled account plus a logged-in victim, and presumes at least one client without `change_email_redirect_url`; the ubiquity of such clients was not measured.

Dependency versions pinned in `shared_versions.gradle` (spring-security-oauth 2.3.0, spring-security-saml 1.0.4, jackson 2.9.8, log4j2 2.11.1) may carry their own known issues that were outside the scope of this source-level review.
I could not establish which single upstream fix commit corresponds to case VUL4J-40; the submitted candidate is the best-supported issue found in this snapshot, not a verified ground-truth match.

rejected_leads.lead: `UaaUrlUtils.uriHasMatchingHost` compares `java.net.URL.getHost()` with `request.getServerName()` before returning `form_redirect_uri` as the post-login redirect (UaaSavedRequestAwareAuthenticationSuccessHandler.java:42, UaaSavedRequestCache.java:95) — a parser differential (e.g. a backslash/userinfo form whose Java host is the UAA host but whose browser host is the attacker) could bypass the allowlist.
rejected_leads.reason: The bypass depends on unspecified java.net.URL authority parsing (backslash inside the authority) that I could not verify from the snapshot, and the reviewed code path additionally requires the victim to submit the login form with the attacker's hidden field. Left as an unconfirmed lead rather than the candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: `AntPathRedirectResolver.redirectMatches` delegates non-wildcard registrations to `DefaultRedirectResolver` (which the repository's own tests assert matches any sub-domain, e.g. `http://domain.com` matches `http://subdomain.domain.com`), and `isValidRegisteredRedirectUrl` permits `*` in sub-domain labels.
rejected_leads.reason: The behaviour is explicitly asserted as intended by `AntPathRedirectResolverTests` (`allSubdomainsShouldMatch`), the wildcard cases are constrained by the registration regex (`isValidRegisteredRedirectUrl`), and the library-internal matching logic is not present in the snapshot, so no vulnerable-vs-intended delta could be demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: `WhitelistLogoutHandler` uses the client's registered redirect URIs (selected by an attacker-supplied `client_id`) as an allowlist for the logout `redirect` parameter, and `isInternalRedirect` accepts any target that merely `startsWith` the reconstructed request URL (WhitelistLogoutHandler.java:66-88).
rejected_leads.reason: `findMatchingRedirectUri` is called with the non-null default target URL (`/login` by default from `Links.Logout`), so an unmatched value falls back to the safe default; the internal-redirect `startsWith` check stays on the same host for all constructions I could form. Not elevated to a candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: `CorsFilter.isAllowedOrigin` / `isAllowedRequestUri` use `Pattern.matcher(value).find()` (substring match) rather than a full match (CorsFilter.java:317-341), while the bundled example configuration in `uaa.yml` is anchored and implies full-match intent.
rejected_leads.reason: Exploitation requires a deployment whose allowed-origin regex is unanchored; the filter never emits `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`, so the practical impact is limited and configuration-dependent. Rejected for lack of a source-level attacker-controlled path.

rejected_leads.lead: `ScimUserSelfUpdateAllowed` exists but is referenced nowhere, and the SCIM XML authorizes `/Users/*` PUT/PATCH for the owner via `@self.isUserSelf(request,1)` only (scim-endpoints.xml:231-232), so a user may change their own `verified`/`active`/`origin`/`externalId` fields.
rejected_leads.reason: `JdbcScimUserProvisioning.update` (lines 244-265) does not persist `authorities`/group membership, so no direct privilege escalation is reachable from the body fields; a full account-takeover chain via `externalId`/`origin` was not established from the source.

rejected_leads.lead: `SimpleSearchQueryConverter` concatenates `sortBy` into SQL (`ORDER BY` + mapped value).
rejected_leads.reason: `AbstractQueryable.query` calls `validateOrderBy(queryConverter.map(sortBy))` against field whitelists before conversion, so no injection path was demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: SAML/metadata XML parsing (`SamlIdentityProviderDefinition`, `SamlServiceProviderDefinition`) and external-OIDC id_token handling (`XOAuthAuthenticationManager`) as XXE/signature-bypass candidates.
rejected_leads.reason: DOCTYPE is rejected before parsing and entity expansion is disabled, and the OIDC path verifies signature, issuer, audience and expiry, so no defect was identified there.

rejected_leads.lead: Cross-zone token/client access (multitenancy) and token listing/revocation endpoints.
rejected_leads.reason: All reviewed JDBC statements filter by `identity_zone_id`, zone-scoped expressions (`hasScopeInAuthZone`) are used, and `/oauth/token/list/**` and `/oauth/token/revoke/**` are constrained by scope rules plus `IsSelfCheck`, so no gap was demonstrated.

summary: Cloud Foundry UAA (4.28.0-SNAPSHOT, Spring Boot 1.5.17 era) reviewed as a defensive source assessment. I focused on authentication/authorization, redirect handling, SCIM/OAuth endpoints, filters and XML security rules. The strongest source-substantiated issue is an open-redirect chain in the email-change verification flow: `EmailChangeEmailService.completeVerification` persists a client-supplied `redirect_uri` into the expiring code and then calls `findMatchingRedirectUri(registeredUris, requestedRedirectUri, changeEmailRedirectUrl)` with a fallback that is normally null; `UaaUrlUtils.findMatchingRedirectUri` returns the *requested* URI whenever the fallback is null (the code's own Javadoc labels this case "OPEN REDIRECT"), so the client whitelist is bypassed. `ChangeEmailController.verifyEmail` then issues a raw Spring `redirect:` view with that value for authenticated callers (and echoes it as `form_redirect_uri` for anonymous callers). Sibling implementations in the same codebase (`UaaResetPasswordService`, `EmailAccountCreationService`, `EmailInvitationsService`, `ChangeEmailEndpoints`) pass a non-null safe default or only use the configured value, which is strong internal counter-evidence that the null fallback here is a defect rather than intent. Reported as a lead with medium confidence, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.
